content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of estimating the causal effects of continuous treatments. To address this problem, the authors propose Adversarial CounterFactual Regression (ACFR), a method which uses a mutual information-based objective and an adversarial game to align the representation of covariates, thus handling the selection bias present in observational datasets. Moreover, ACFR predicts the potential outcomes using a contribution-constraining hypothesis network.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper addresses an important and under-explored problem in the causal inference literature. 
- The paper is well written and the proposed method is thoroughly motivated and well-described. 
- The proposed approach of minimizing the mutual information between the learnt representation and the treatment while at the same time ensuring that the learnt representation is predictive of outcomes is theoretically motivated. 
- ACFR is extensively evaluated in a semi-synthetic set-up. 

Weaknesses:
- While the balancing representation approach is standard in the causal inference literature, one of its drawbacks is that it can remove information about covariates that are both predictive of the treatment and the outcome. Thus, I believe that the paper would benefit from further discussion about this problem. 
- The objective of ACFR contains several hyperparameters ($\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$). The paper would be improved by including a more thorough description of how these hyperparameters are selected in practice.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Novelty: building adversarially balanced representations for treatments effect estimation has been used by several other works which I believe the authors should acknowledge in the related works section [1-3]. Despite this, I believe that the paper uses adversarial balancing in a very principled and appropriate way for estimating the effects of continuous treatments. 
- The paper is clearly written and it provides enough experimental details for reproducibility. 


[1] Du, Xin, et al. "Adversarial balancing-based representation learning for causal effect inference with observational data." Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 35.4 (2021): 1713-1738.
[2] Bica, Ioana, et al. "Estimating counterfactual treatment outcomes over time through adversarially balanced representations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.04083 (2020).
[3] Berrevoets, Jeroen, et al. "OrganITE: Optimal transplant donor organ offering using an individual treatment effect." Advances in neural information processing systems 33 (2020): 20037-20050.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, 

We appreciate your constructive comments. We address your concerns in the following. We address your concerns in the following. If you believe we haven’t addressed all your concerns, we look forward to further discussions with you.

**Q1.While the balancing representation approach is standard in the causal inference literature, one of its drawbacks is that it can remove information about covariates that are both predictive of the treatment and the outcome.**

**A1**. Briefly, ACFR excludes information about instrumental variables (the covariates only predictive of treatment) from the representation and learns to involve information of confounders remaining in the representation in the outcome prediction network as less as possible. 

As discussed in the two last paragraphs of section 3.1, ACFR's encoder, cannot entirely remove the selection bias, i.e. the encoder cannot learn a representation such that $P(T) = P(T|Z)$. Therefore, we expect that the encoder suffices to exclude instrumental variables because removing instrumental variables removal from representation does not hurt outcome prediction. Therefore, information of confounding variables remains in the learned representation.


In order to prevent confounding information from spuriously affecting outcome prediction, we introduced another loss term $L_{co}$. $L_{con}$ is the prediction of outcome from a perturbed representation, a representation that its confounding information is constrained.  This loss term pushes the hypothesis network to be robust to confounding information in the representation, and involve them only when needed. More details can be found in the last two paragraphs of section 3.2.


**Q2.The objective of ACFR contains several hyperparameters ($\gamma$_1 and $\gamma$_2). The paper would be improved by including a more thorough description of how these hyperparameters are selected in practice.**

**A2**. We specified the hyperparameters search range in Appendix A.1, and we used grid search to find the best combination. Moreover, in the revised draft, we have added another experiment along with a discussion in Appendix A.1 to analyze the effect of loss function hyper-parameters on ACFR's performance. 

**Q3. Building adversarially balanced representations for treatments effect estimation has been used by several other works which I believe the authors should acknowledge in the related works section.**

**A3**. In the revised draft, we have added a paragraph in the related works section and we discussed the similarities and differences between our approach and other adversarially balanced representation for causal inference. Consequently, we moved the paragraph corresponding to adversarial domain adaptation to Appendix A.2 due to the page limit.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 2 [1/2]
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, 

We appreciate your constructive comments. We address your concerns in the following. We hope that our responses will increase your enthusiasm for our paper. If you believe we haven’t addressed all your concerns, we look forward to further discussions with you.

**Q1.The proposed method ruled out unobserved confounders (in Assumption a) and Figure 1. If so, why do the authors propose to balance latent representation Z, but not observed covariates X?**

**A1**. Existence of confounders exhibits selection bias ($P(T) \ne P(T|X)$) in a causal observational dataset. Balancing the observed covariates (X) in order to mitigate the selection bias has been widely studied in the causal inference literature. Representation learning is one of the approaches for covariate balancing. In principle, in the representation learning approach, we aim to map the context information of units from covariate space into representation space using a neural network (encoder) such that the assigned treatment ($T$) to units is not distinguishable from their representation ($Z$),  i.e. the distribution of different treatment groups look similar in the representation space. The described representation is called balanced. Please note that the representation $Z$ for units is not given and we do not balance it explicitly, but we optimize the parameter of the neural network such that the resulting representation satisfies the balancing condition. 

If the balanced representation space has the capacity that allows us to predict factual outcomes accurately from it, we would then ensure accuracy on counterfactual outcomes as well. This is because the counterfactual outcome prediction will not be correlated with the actual assigned treatment of the unit (thanks to the balanced property of representation). 
This approach proposed in [1], has achieved state-of-the-art results for treatment effect estimation, particularly for individual-level estimation. Furthermore, in a seminal paper [2], authors have provided a generalization-error upper bound (Lemma 1) on counterfactual prediction which theoretically justifies the effectiveness of representation learning for causal inference.

**Q2.What is the formal definition of I(T, Z; phi) and I(Z, Y | T; phi) when they are first introduced on page 2? Why the parameters phi are shared in these two notations?**

**A2**. As explained above, the representation $Z$ should satisfy two properties. 1) Its dependence on the treatment variable should be minimized. 2) It should not lose the expressive power for outcome prediction. One of our main contributions is to characterize these properties by mutual information terms, $I(T, Z; \phi)$ and $I(Z, Y |T; \phi)$ respectively. We have included the formal definition of mutual information of two variables in the footnote of the revised version. The reason that mutual information terms have been shown with parameter $\phi$, is that they are defined between distribution $Z$ and some other distribution. $Z$ is determined by an encoder with parameter $\phi$, and hence the mutual information terms are parameterized by $\phi$. This notation is used to show that mutual information terms have to be optimized over this parameter.

**Q3. A theoretical analysis of the proposed approach is lacking. For example, can the proposed approach identify and consistently estimate the conditional average treatment effect mu(x, t) = E[Y | X = x, T = t]?**

**A3**. The theoretical guarantees for deep individual treatment effect estimators have been in the form of generalization-error bounds. See the generalization bound in [2] for binary treatment and in [3] for continuous treatment settings. 
The generalization-error bounds have been used to design a specific loss function for the deep estimator. We have discussed these resulting loss functions in the third paragraph of the Introduction in detail, explaining why they cannot be effective in a continuous treatment setting. The loss function we have used for our model, ACFR, does not guarantee the minimization of outcome estimation error. 
Nonetheless, we respectfully disagree that theoretical analysis is lacking. Existing terms in our loss function (Equation 12) are theoretically motivated and explicitly derived to optimize the mutual information objective (Equation 1).
The mutual information approach allowed us to theoretically justify the adversarial balancing idea. Specifically, in section 3.1, we argued how the adversarial balancing approach results in alignment between the expectation of $P(T)$ and $P(T|Z)$ distributions. 
Furthermore, in section 3.2 we showed that minimizing $L_{fo}$ ensures maximizing $I(Z, Y |T)$. We have demonstrated that previous representation learning methods can all be viewed as $I(Z, Y |T)$ maximizers, and they vary with respect to their architecture design for the variational distribution $q_{\theta}(y|z, t)$ (Equation 9.2)

content.strength_and_weaknesses: I address strengths and weakness is the context of the categories below
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

1) Spaces are frequently missing. Please fix this in the next draft.
2) Why does MISE integrate t with respect to the uniform density?
3) Why is PE a relevant metric in the experiments?

Quality

1) Under the stated assumptions, mu(x,t)=E[Y|X=x,T=t]; the authors are proposing an estimator for nonparametric regression. Nonetheless, the authors propose a loss that encourages good fit of regression (eq. 11) and penalizes overfitting of the generalized propensity score (eq. 7). Theoretical results would clarify in which scenarios this loss would improve performance relative to a simpler regression loss. However, the paper does not have theoretical results.

2) The intuition is interesting

Novelty

1) There is a great deal of work on entropy balancing in dose response estimation, none of which is cited. See “End-to-End Balancing for Causal Continuous Treatment-Effect Estimation” (Bahadori- Tchetgen-Heckerman ICML 2022) for a recent review. This literature does have some consistency guarantees, which this paper does not. I would like the authors to cite and compare with these prior works. In particular, please say in which scenarios the proposal would work better

2) For the specific scenario of individual treatment effect estimation of continuous treatment, prior works exist with consistency guarantees, e.g. “Kernel Methods for Causal Functions” (Singh-Xu-Gretton arXiv 2020), which also have a balancing interpretation. I would like the authors to cite these prior works and explain in which scenarios the proposal would work better.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 3 [1/3]
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, 

We appreciate your constructive comments. We address your concerns in the following. We hope that our responses will increase your enthusiasm for our paper. If you believe we haven’t addressed all your concerns, we look forward to further discussions with you.

**Q1. Discussion of improvement relative to previous work on entropy balancing and on individual treatment effect estimation of continuous treatment. I would like the authors to cite these prior works and explain in which scenarios the proposal would work better.**

**A1**.
First of all, we should emphasize that our work belongs to the balanced **representation learning** approach for the treatment effect estimation problem established by [1]. Entropy Balancing [2]  belongs to the re-weighting approach and has been proposed to address the problem of extreme weights. In the balanced representation learning approach, we encode the unit's context information from covariate space $X$ into a lower-dimensional latent space $Z$ using a neural network (NN) in order to mitigate the selection bias. The term **balanced** in this context refers to aligning the distribution of different treatment groups so that they look similar and one cannot predict a unit's assigned treatment from its representation encoding. Whereas sample re-weighting methods such as Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW) and Entropy Balancing are based on creating a pseudo-population in the covariate space using instance weights such that the covariate and the assigned treatment be approximately independent. Therefore, the approach we have taken in this work is fundamentally different from entropy balancing or sample re-weighting in general.

We discussed two aspects of the difference between balanced representation learning and entropy balancing in the following:
1) In entropy balancing, methods commonly use some set of kernel functions defined over the covariate space in order to force independence between covariates and treatments. However, in balanced representation learning, methods learn these functions by optimizing neural network parameters over a loss term (we have used the minimax loss term to this end).
2) Methods in sample re-weighting and covariate balancing directly estimate the treatment effect quantity using the obtained weights, whereas representation learning methods predict the potential outcomes given the representation, and subsequently estimate the treatment effect. Therefore, their theoretical guarantees are in the form of error-bound on estimated potential outcomes [3].

We believe it would be interesting to compare causal inference methods that have been proposed based on different approaches. Nonetheless, it is common for a proposed representation learning method to be compared against other deep learning baselines since these methods have achieved the best experimental performance on many tasks in causal inference [4]. Similar to previous works [1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], we have compared ACFR against baselines that are classified as a representation learning approach. Varying Coefficient Network [7] is the state-of-the-art for average-level continuous treatment effect estimation. Dose-Response Network [6] is one of the first deep learning methods that regarded treatment as a continuous variable, and finally, CounterFactual Regression [3] is the state-of-the-art balanced representation method for binary treatment (we have modified its architecture to support continuous treatment).

content.title: Thank you for these responses
content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for these thoughtful responses.

I appreciate the empirical comparison using different losses, including a simple regression loss.

The additional discussion is helpful for a broad audience to understand why non-standard metrics are used for empirical evaluation.

In my view, the fundamental issue that remains is that the paper does not articulate assumptions that imply consistency. Intuition is helpful and serves an important purpose, but only a formalization of the intuition can lead to a satisfying explanation of what the proposed balancing really means--especially since so many notions of balancing are popular in causal inference, and they occasionally coincide.

Even some basic propositions would help in this regard.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 3 [2/3]
content.comment:
**Q2.Comparison of the proposed loss function with simpler regression loss. In particular, please say in which scenarios the proposal would work better.**

**A2**. We are not sure whether we understood your concern about a comparison against simpler regression loss. More explanation will be helpful. 

Note that we have designed a loss function for our deep learning model which is consisted of three terms: $L_{fo}$, $L_{adv}$, and $L_{con}$. $L_{fo}$ is the regression loss for the predicted outcome which we think is what you meant. $L_{fo}$ has been optimized using the parameters of a neural network which is a powerful hypothesis class compared to simpler regression losses. In the following, we argue why other terms in ACFR loss function, $L_{adv}$ and $L_{con}$ are necessary for the model.

Optimizing network parameters only with a regression loss for outcome prediction results in overfitting the factual outcomes.  In fact, One can summarize the entire literature of balanced representation learning in modifications on this regression loss in order to make the model generalizable to counterfactuals. Furthermore, we have included a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model into our baselines which is trained only with the outcome prediction regression loss $L_{fo}$. ACFR and all other representation learning methods outperformed MLP regardless of the amount of selection bias and the semi-synthetic dataset (Table 2). Also, we would like to refer you to section 4.3 and Figure 4 (source of gain analysis), which show the contribution of our proposed terms to the performance. 

**Q3.Why does MISE integrate t with respect to uniform density? Why is PE a relevant metric in the experiments?**

**A3**. In order to clarify what each metric measures, we provided a dose-response interpretation of the continuous ITE problem in the following. 


Based on the data generating process shown in Table 1, we collected pairs of $(x_i, t_i, y_i)_{i=1}^N$ for $N$ units and they were given to a continuous ITE model.  Following [8], without loss of generality, we assumed treatments are bounded in $[0, 1]$, and $p(t|x)$ follows a $Beta$ distribution.
The outcome generating function is a function of $x$ and $t$ (for example for TCGA dataset we have: $y = \mu(x, t) = 10 (v_1^Tx + 12v_2^Txt -12 v_3^Txt^2)$ ). Fixing $x$ to $x_i$  results in a dose-response function, which shows how changing the dose (treatment) changes the response (outcome) for unit $i$. ($t_i, y_i$) is the only point in unit $i$'s dose-response function that is given to ACFR, and the goal is to predict the entire function.
In other words, $y_i$ is the factual outcome of unit $i$, and all other outcomes associated with any treatment in the range $[0, 1]$ except $t_i$ are counterfactuals. **Since we have no preference for the potential outcome of some specific treatments and performance on all potential outcomes are equally important for us, we assumed the marginal distribution of the treatment to be uniform, $p(t) \sim U(0, 1)$.**

Therefore, having $\mu(x_i, t)$ as the ground-truth dose-response function of unit $i$, and $f(x_i, t)$ as the dose-response function for a unit $i$ estimated by model $f$, we want to measure the squared difference between these functions over the entire range of treatment $[0, 1]$. Therefore, we integrate the squared difference over the treatment range.

$$\int_{0}^1[\mu(x_i, t) - f(x_i, t)]^2 dt$$
Averaging the above formula over all units, we obtain MISE formula. In the following, we will explain the policy error metric and its interpretation:

Understanding what the best treatment for each unit is, depends on the specification of outcome in an observational dataset. Without loss of generality, we assumed the higher the outcome, the better its associated treatment is. As explained above, a continuous ITE model $f(x, t)$ predicts $N$ dose-response functions for $N$ units of the dataset. The policy of a model for unit $i$ is the treatment with the greatest outcome
 in the predicted dose-response function of the unit,  defined as $argmax_{t}f(x_i, t)$. The optimal policy for unit $i$ is similarly defined as $argmax \mu (x_i, t)$ using the ground-truth dose-response function.
**In some applications such as precision medicine, one might only be interested in having a predictive model that has a policy close to optimal since we want to prescribe the best treatment. In order to compare different predictive models in terms of their predicted policy, Policy Error (PE) metric can be used.**
PE for unit $i$ is the squared difference between the highest outcome in the d-truth dose-response function and the outcome of the ground-truth dose-response function when treatment is the policy of the predictive model. In other words, it measures the sub-optimality of the model.
